<reason>A tight, high-quality clash that turned entirely on what "same basic terms" means. PRO won it by drawing and holding the standards-vs-terms distinction (the exam a product passes vs. the rules it is sold under), anchored by the pork/beef/poultry analogy—different tests, same basic regime—which CON never squarely refuted. PRO also turned CON's own irradiated-food and engineered-salmon examples into the model it defends (tailored approval, then ordinary food law) and, crucially, showed that CON's B1.5/B1.6 concessions (no bans, harmonize when evidence earns it) and B4.3 answer (criteria published at approval, then parity) converge on the motion itself. CON was sharp and inventive—the "airplane with a car crash test" image, the reckless-or-self-defeating dilemma, the voluntary/mandatory label distinction, and the closing's "a steer cannot drift" point were real pressure. But CON's case leaned heavily on a strict reading of "same" that made the motion "empty," a meta-argument PRO defused by showing CON was merely specifying what "safety standards are met" means. CON's closing also strained against its own B4.3 by suggesting parity never arrives. PRO's clipped opening is a small execution cost but doesn't change the outcome.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Turn 3 [A2.3]–[A2.6]: PRO seized CON's own salmon/irradiation examples and the pork/beef/poultry analogy to split "safety standards" from "basic terms," reframing the whole debate so that CON's later three post-approval rules could be characterized as either safety standards or existing meat-regime functions.</best_rebuttal>
